title: Parity Analysis for Coin Representation
approach_explanation: The problem asks whether we can express $n = 2x + ky$ for some non-negative integers $x$ and $y$. We can break this down by analyzing the parity of $k$ and $n$. Since $2x$ is always even, the parity of $n$ is determined solely by $ky$. If $k$ is odd, we can always choose $y$ such that $ky$ matches the parity of $n$ (either $0$ or $1$ times $k$), and the remaining amount $n - ky$ will be even, allowing it to be covered by $2x$. If $k$ is even, $ky$ is always even, meaning $n$ must be even to be representable. Finally, if $k = 1$, any $n$ can be represented using $y = n$.

code_breakdown.explanation: Includes standard headers, sets up fast I/O, and reads the number of test cases $t$.

Reads $n$ and $k$ as 64-bit signed integers (`long long`) to prevent overflow given $10^{18}$ constraints. Evaluates the ternary condition: if $k == 1$, or $k$ is odd ($k 	ext{ % } 2 == 1$), or both $k$ and $n$ are even ($k 	ext{ % } 2 == 0 	ext{ and } n 	ext{ % } 2 == 0$), prints 'YES'; otherwise prints 'NO'.

complexity_analysis.time_justification: The solution loops through each of the $t$ test cases and performs a constant number of arithmetic and logical operations in $O(1)$ time per test case.
complexity_analysis.space_justification: Only a few scalar variables (`t`, `n`, `k`) of type `long long` and `int` are used, which require constant auxiliary memory.

strengths: Uses `long long` to prevent integer overflow for $10^{18}$.
Per test case time complexity is optimal at $O(1)$.
edge_cases_handled: Large values of $n$ and $k$ up to $10^{18}$ handled correctly via 64-bit integers.

Handles cases where $k$ is larger than $n$ implicitly via problem constraints ($k 
e 2$).
Handles both odd and even parity branches exhaustively.
best_practices_feedback: Consider using explicit conditional blocks `if-else` instead of nested ternary operators for better readability.
Avoid `#include<bits/stdc++.h>` in production environments for compilation speed, though it is standard in competitive programming.

optimization_and_alternatives.tradeoffs: Using bitwise operations like `(n & 1)` instead of modulo `(n % 2)` can micro-optimize performance, though modern compilers optimize modulo by powers of two automatically.
